chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Abdullah, from Ahmad ibn Abu Abdullah, from Yahya ibn Ibrahim ibn Abu al-Bilad, from his father, from his grandfather, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

A Bedouin came to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) and said, 'Teach me a deed by which I may enter Paradise.' He (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'Feed people and spread the greeting of peace.' The Bedouin said, 'I cannot endure that.' He (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'Do you have camels?' He said, 'Yes.' He (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'So look after a camel and provide water for it for a family who do not drink water except intermittently, so that perhaps your camel will not be exhausted and your water-skin will not be damaged until Paradise becomes obligatory for you.'
ai.seo_question: What practical deed did the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) suggest for someone who found general acts of worship too difficult?
ai.summary: In this hadith from al-Kafi, the Prophet (peace be upon him) tailors spiritual guidance to the Bedouin’s capacity, offering a manageable act of charity—providing water to a family intermittently while caring for a camel—as a sustainable path to Paradise. This reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on gradualism (tadrij) and the practicality of worship, where consistent, small deeds are valued over overwhelming, short-lived efforts. The narrative underscores the importance of animal welfare and communal care as integral components of faith.
